text:
The racer's start-line countdown goes off for nobody — three, two, one — and both front seats sit empty, the wheel jerking left on its own for a ghost that already took the first corner clean. Aura flipped it to attract mode an hour ago and hasn't looked back at it since. Awen has looked at it four times. There's a dead spot in the steering column, off-center, maybe four degrees left, and she keeps not mentioning it.

"You're doing the thing." Aura hasn't turned around. She's at the change counter with the takeout spread open, one carton already gutted, chopsticks going. "The face. At my machine."

"It has a dead spot."

"It's had a dead spot since before you."

"I know." Awen crosses to her. The whole room is dark except the cabinets, and the cabinets throw the only weather in the place — red off the racer, a cold blue wash from the rhythm cab in the corner, its marquee light still ticking at the ballast the way it has for months. "That's not a defense. That's a timeline."

The chopsticks come up over Aura's shoulder without her looking. Awen takes them blind; they've done this enough that the handoff just lands. She steals from the gutted carton on principle, which is the rule, the carton Aura opens first is the one they fight over.

"Off the cab, by the way," Aura says. "House rules. Dumplings stay off the Street Fighter cab."

"We're nowhere near the—"

"Pre-emptive."

Awen's bag is on the counter where she set it down, the twice-taped corner of the thing inside just showing past the zip. She turns it so the corner doesn't show. Not the point of putting it away; the point is she looked. The joint isn't true yet — the evening still has ornament on it, and she can't hand it over with ornament still on.

Aura came around the end of the counter a minute ago at half her usual speed. Half. Awen clocked it and said nothing, because you don't reach for a thing somebody's carrying carefully before they've set it down; you let them find the counter. Whatever it is, Aura will race straight past it about six more times before she lets it land. That's fine. Awen has all night and a dead carton to defend.

"Racer," Aura says. "Right now. You're down two in the room and I can feel you not caring, which is worse than losing."

"I'm eating."

"Bring it." Already moving — of course she's already moving, she's at the seats before the sentence lands, dropping into the left one, the good one, the one without the dead spot. "Loser gets the last dumpling taken from them at a time of my choosing."

Awen looks at the wheel in the right seat. Four degrees. She could fix it in ten minutes with the machine cold and would enjoy every one of them.

She sets the carton down and gets in anyway.

The light-tree drops green and Aura is gone. Not fast — gone, a whole car-length up the track before Awen's even cleared the start gate, her ghost-line the perfect one, the one the machine wants you to drive.

Awen doesn't chase the ghost. She drives the wheel she's got. Four degrees of slack before the front end answers, so she turns four degrees into nothing, early, feeds the correction in before each corner asks for it. The car goes where she meant instead of where the column's backlash would send it. It's slower on paper. It's honest. And that's worth about a length a lap, corner after corner.

"You're doing something." Aura doesn't look over. She never looks over; she watches the road like it owes her money. "I can hear you doing something over there. Stop it."

"Driving."

"Sure. That's your fixing-my-machine-with-your-face sound — I'd know it in my sleep."

"Can't fix it from here." Awen takes the hairpin. The wheel fights her the way it always does and she lets it, hands already four degrees ahead of the fight. "I'm just being polite to it."

Aura's shoulder drops a half-inch on the next straight. Awen has seen that shoulder a hundred times; it used to mean the race was over. Tonight she just files it, keeps her line, and comes out of the chicane closer than she went in.

"Artemis drove like you," Aura says, apropos of nothing — or of the gap Awen's been eating into all lap. "Never met a straight shot she wouldn't complicate. Drove me up a wall."

"You didn't have cars."

"Chariots. Same principle, worse suspension." The gap holds; the gap shrinks. "She'd have loved you. It would've been unbearable. Two of you 'respecting the mechanism' at me while I—" the last corner comes up and Aura takes it flat-out fast, the ghost-line, the greedy one, "—won."

She doesn't win. Not clean, anyway. Her fast line runs her wide at exit, one hair wide, the width of the slack Awen's been turning early against all lap, and there's a gap on the inside exactly one car wide — and Awen is already in it, four degrees ahead of the fight, the front end for once pointed exactly where she put it, drawing level at the line with the machine that's been lying to her all night doing, at last, precisely what she told it to

"That didn't happen."

Aura's out of the seat before the replay finishes drawing it, standing over the screen like standing closer will renegotiate the result. The photo-finish freezes both cars at the line and then, unkindly, gives it to the inside one by a bumper.

"It's on the board." Awen stays put a second longer, hands still on the wheel, the four degrees of slack gone quiet now she's stopped fighting it. "You can glare at it as long as you want. It'll keep saying the same thing."

"You drove the broken one."

"I drove the one nobody else wanted. That's just manners."

Aura makes a sound that isn't a word. Then, with enormous dignity, she reaches over and taps the cabinet twice — some private thing, machine to owner — and steps back. "Fine. Invoking the sulk. House rules: one song's length, and you don't get to talk to me during it."

"You wrote that rule so you'd have a legal way to lose."

"I wrote that rule because I'm a genius." She's already drifting toward the rhythm cab in the corner, the one whose marquee keeps ticking its broken little pulse, weight up on the balls of her feet again — the sulk apparently involves picking a song loud enough to be a statement. "Dumpling's still yours, by the way. Whenever. I pay my debts. I just do it resentfully."

"I know. It's one of your best qualities."

"It's my worst and my best at once. I'm complicated." She reaches the rhythm cab. Doesn't start it. Her hand goes flat on the panel and stays there, and for a second — one whole second, which on Aura is a geological event — she just stands with her back to Awen, like there's something to read in the flicker.

Awen watches the back of her not start the song.

Then Aura says, "Hey, so—" at completely normal speed. And stops. And starts a different sentence, faster, the real thing — whatever it was — folded back up and put away: "—you are going to want to sit down for how badly I'm about to lose to you at this next, too, out of spite."

"You said no talking during the sulk."

"The sulk hasn't started. I haven't picked the song." She finally jabs the panel, and the cabinet wakes up loud, some four-on-the-floor thing with too many arrows, and she rolls her shoulders like a woman cracking her knuckles before a heist. "Now it's started. Get over here and lose politely."

The high-score table scrolls up while the song loads, and there it is, third from the top: AWN, 942,110, a date four months gone. Awen's tag. The night she took this exact cabinet off Aura and has not once let it drop since.

She barely notices her own name. What holds her is the company it's keeping — the two lines above and the eleven below, all Aura's, AUR and ARA and one Awen won't dignify by reading twice, the whole board three tags deep, same as the building itself. Except that one row. Four months. Awen has watched Aura wipe a stranger's record off the fighting cab the way you'd straighten a picture in your own hallway. And she left this. A worse score than a dozen of her own, sitting third from the top in her own house, and four months on she still hasn't cleared it.

Awen doesn't say anything about that. She files it — she's filing a lot tonight — with the carried thing and the covered sentence, the parts of Aura she hasn't finished reading yet.

"You're stalling." Aura drops onto the pad beside her, shoulder to shoulder, already thumbing the difficulty up past where it's polite. "I can hear you getting sentimental at my leaderboard. Stop dating the machine. Date me."

"I'm studying the competition."

"You're third."

"I'm studying how you'll feel in a minute about being second."

The song hits and the talking stops, because this one you can't do slow. Arrows come up faster than banter, and for a while there's only the double thud of four feet on two pads and the light off the screen going frantic on both their faces. Aura is better — Aura is always better, she's three thousand years of hand-eye and no patience for a thing she can't win — but Awen is beside her and keeping up, and every so often their elbows knock on a crossover and neither of them fixes their spacing.

The song lands its last note. Aura won it; the screen says so; neither of them looks at the screen.

They're both breathing hard. Aura's ponytail has fully lost its argument with the evening and she doesn't push it back, and she's looking at Awen instead of the board she just topped, still up on the balls of her feet like the song might come back around.

"Okay," Awen says. It comes out smaller than she meant it to. She reaches into her bag.

The wrapping's been off and on so many times the tape has stopped believing in itself; it gives without a sound. Then it's just the thing in her palm, in the blue light off the cabinet, and Awen makes herself hold it out flat instead of explaining it.

It's a key. Brass, because brass forgives being handled and only gets better for it. The blade she cut herself, by hand, on the mill in the back of the shop, to the pattern of one particular lock. The bow — the part you hold — she spent longer on than she'll say: an openwork wind rose, the eight points of the compass fanning from the center, and between them enamel the exact deep blue the cabinets throw in a dark room. It took her three tries to get the blue to lie down flat. She got it on the third.

She doesn't say what it opens. She wants to see if Aura gets there on her own.

Aura takes it, and doesn't say anything, which is the first strange thing — Aura fills a silence the way nature fills a vacuum, on principle, and she isn't filling this one. She turns the key over once. Her thumb finds the wind rose and stays on it a second, and Awen thinks, she likes the pretty part, everyone likes the pretty part —

and then Aura turns it back and looks at the blade. The working end. Runs the pad of her thumb along the cuts, the specific ones, the ones that fit exactly one lock in the world, and the fast goes out of her face.

"This is your shop." Not a question. Slow — one whole unhurried sentence, and Awen has never once heard her talk that slow. "You made me a key to your shop."

"Front and back — same key. The back door sticks; you have to lift while you turn. I keep meaning to plane it down and I never—"

She stops. She was about to say she never gets around to it, and it isn't even true — she likes the door exactly that stubborn. But Aura has closed her hand around the key, all the way, the wind rose vanishing into her fist, and she's looking at Awen, gone still on both feet for once, and a sentence about a sticking door is the least interesting thing in the building.

Aura looks down at her own closed hand, then back up. "You know I've got every record in this place." Her thumb moves once across the top of her fist. "Every machine, every tag. This is number one now. I'm not standing it on a shelf."

She's got a carabiner of keys at her hip — arcade, back room, the roll-gate out front — and she threads Awen's onto it right there, brass ringing once against steel.

"Okay." The ring drops back against her hip. "Put the bag down."

Awen puts the bag down.

And then Aura kisses her — or she kisses Aura; it has never once been possible to say who starts it, they have argued about this, there's no replay to check — and it isn't a first kiss, they're miles past first kisses, but there's a cold little edge of brass caught between them at the hip and Aura, the fastest thing in the world, is kissing her like there's no queue behind it and nowhere after this she has to be, and that

— and that does it. Awen's hand finds the back of Aura's neck sure as a light switch in the dark, no looking needed, and pulls her in past whatever careful thing she was still doing. The key's edge digs in between them and neither of them moves it. Aura makes a sound into her mouth that isn't a word, and Awen swallows it and gives one back.

Aura kisses all-in, no pacing left in her now — the slow gone, the fast back but aimed — both hands going up into Awen's hair and working the pin loose until the whole dark weight of it comes down, and she laughs against Awen's mouth, the pin still shut in her fist like she won it.

"That was a good pin," Awen says.

"I'll build you a better one." A lie; she couldn't build a sandwich; they both know it and neither cares. She's already walking Awen backward — past the dark cabinets, toward the stairs at the back — the bag left on the floor, the key cold at her hip. "I'll build you a whole—"

Awen kisses her quiet before she has to finish lying about it.

They go.

The upstairs is one room, a bed, and a window over the dark cabinets, and Awen sees none of it — Aura has her by the front of the shirt on the last three steps and hasn't let go at the top.

She gets the staff jacket off Aura's shoulders, the ridiculous ironic staff jacket, and it hits the floor. The shirt under it goes the same way. Aura's fast everywhere at once — that's the whole thing about her, hands at Awen's waist and her mouth at Awen's jaw and her weight already tipping them toward the bed — and Awen plants a flat hand on Aura's sternum and holds her off a second, just to look.

She looks. Aura lets her, barely, everything in her voting to move. The cabinet light comes up cold and blue through the window and lays a line down her — collarbone, the color already up her chest, the dip of her waist — and Awen takes her in the way she takes in anything she's about to put her hands on, finding where it wants to be touched before she touches it.

"You're measuring me," Aura says.

"I'm admiring you. There's math in admiring. Hold still."

"I don't hold still."

"I've noticed. Do it anyway."

And she does. One second. Two. Long enough for Awen to lean in and set her mouth to the heat at the top of Aura's chest and feel the breath go out of her all at once and come back ragged.

Then Aura's hands find the hem of Awen's shirt, and the looking's done, they're both through being patient—

Naked, Aura is all the things the jacket hides. The runner's spring still in her thighs. An old silvered scar under one breast that Awen has asked about twice and been told two different lies. The color that was up her chest is down her whole front now, and she's warm — she runs a few degrees hot, always has.

Awen puts her on the bed and takes her time. She kisses down Aura's throat, the notch at the base of it, the inner curve of each breast, and draws a nipple into her mouth until Aura's spine lifts off the sheet and a sound comes out of her with no words in it and no speed either.

"Awen—"

"I know. I've got the whole night." She doesn't hurry. She kisses down the flat of Aura's stomach, the muscle jumping under her mouth, the hip that turns up toward her, and settles between Aura's thighs, where the heat is, where she's already slick and open and lifting toward Awen's mouth.

She's learned this body over months — where slow works, and where Aura needs her to quit being an engineer about it and just go — and she gives both, in the order that undoes her: long flat strokes of her tongue until Aura's hips are chasing her, then two fingers pressed in slow and curled up to the place that pulls her whole body taut as a strung line, and her mouth closed over her, no mercy in it now.

Aura, who narrates everything, has stopped narrating. Down to single syllables, then to none. Both hands are fisted in Awen's hair, holding on, and her thighs are shaking on either side of Awen's head, and Awen feels the exact moment the tension crosses over — the stillness right before — and stays with her through it, steady, relentless, until Aura comes apart around her fingers with a cry the empty arcade downstairs throws back up at them, faint, once.

Awen stays where she is, gentling her down, until the shaking quiets to the odd aftershock and Aura's hand goes loose in her hair.

Then, from somewhere above her, wrecked and slow: "Okay. New record."

Aura sprawls half on top of her like she's claiming ground, and Awen works the knots out of her hair, the ones they just put there. The cabinet-blue comes up through the window and the empty arcade hums its after-hours hum below them, and for a while neither of them keeps score of anything.

Then Aura reaches down over the side of the bed, digs her phone out of the jacket on the floor, and hands it over without a word.

It's open to a note. The title is just a date, eight months back. Under it, a list.

first night — drank the bad well whiskey neat, didn't blink. asked which cab I loved best and called my bluff when I lied

took my SFII ghost round two. informed me my hinge was loud

rhythm cab, 942k. have not cleared it. not going to

owe her one (1) dumpling, indefinite, on purpose

It goes on. Months of it. Every record Awen's ever taken off her in that room, every number — and threaded between the numbers the other things, a whiskey, a hinge, a dumpling held hostage, logged in the same flat hand as the scores.

Awen scrolls. She doesn't trust her hands not to do something stupid, so she keeps them on the phone.

"You keep a scoreboard of me," she says. Quiet. Exact.

"I keep a scoreboard of everything." Aura's chin is on her chest, watching her read it. "You're just winning."

Aura takes the phone back and doesn't look at it, sets it face-down on the mattress like the evidence it is. She's up on one elbow now, and for once not doing anything with the rest of her — no bounce, no drift, no reaching for the next thing.

"Okay, so." She stops. Starts again, slower, visibly making herself do it. "I'm going to say a thing at normal-person speed, and you don't get to make fun of the speed."

"I would never."

"You would immediately." She does it anyway, slow, each word set down exactly where she wants it. "I've queued solo a long time. Longer than you'd believe if I told you the number, which I'm not going to. And I don't want a teammate for tonight." Her thumb finds the brass key on the carabiner at the edge of the bed, turns the wind rose once. "I want the standing slot. Player two, permanent, no expiry. You."

Awen discovers she's been holding her breath. She lets it out.

She reaches over and turns the phone back face-up.

"Add a line," she says. Quiet. Exact. "I saw the 942k months ago. Knew you'd left it up on purpose. Never said anything — because I wanted to keep it too."

Then she takes the brass key, and the whole loaded carabiner with it, and folds Aura's hand shut around the lot — her shop, Aura's keys, Aura's hand, all of it in the one fist — and holds it there.

Aura lasts about ninety seconds of holding still before the fast comes back into her, all at once.

"Okay. Downstairs. Rematch, best of five, and this time I'm not going easy on you out of respect for the moment we just had."

"You went easy on me?"

"I will revise history, it's a house rule—" But she doesn't get up. And Awen doesn't let go of the fist she's holding, and for a minute the rematch just sits there being a thing they'll definitely do later.

Below them the cabinets run their attract loops in the dark, every one set to free play, keeping their own scores for nobody, patient as the woman who owns them has never once been. The blue light comes up through the floor. Down there a start-line countdown goes off for no one — three, two, one — and neither of them moves to answer it.
